Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 1:

(Surat al-Saffat is Meccan, and its verses number one hundred and eighty-two.)

﴿By those who range themselves in ranks, rank upon rank﴾ is an oath by Allah, Exalted and Majestic, by the multitudes of angels who form the ranks, on the understanding that what is intended is the act itself without regard to an object of the act; or [the meaning is] "those who range [themselves]" themselves, i.e., those who arrange them (the ranks) in the line of rows by standing in their known stations, as indicated by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾. On these two meanings rests His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, we are those who stand in ranks﴾. It has been said: "those who range" refers to their feet in prayer; and it has been said: their wings in the air.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 2:

﴿By those who drive forcefully, driving⁠﴾ That is: those who perform the driving (zajr), or those who drive what has been entrusted to them to drive, of the heavenly and earthly bodies and others, in a manner befitting the one being driven. Among that is the driving of servants away from sins, and the driving of the devils away from whispering (waswasa) and misguidance (ighwa), and away from eavesdropping (istiraq al-sam'), as will come. "Safffan" (ranks) and "zajran" (driving) are two verbal nouns (masdar) emphasizing what precedes them, meaning: an exceptional ranking and an eloquent driving. As for the mention (dhikr) of them in His Exalted saying:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 3:**

﴿فالتّالِياتِ ذِكْرًا﴾ The object (*maf'ul*, the grammatical object) of *al-tali'at* is implied: *al-tali'at dhikran* (those that recite a remembrance) of great standing, from the signs of God Most High and His books sent down upon the prophets, peace be upon them, and other than these, [such as] glorification (*tasbih*), sanctification (*taqdis*), praise (*tahmid*) and exaltation (*tamjid*).

It was also said: it is itself a verbal noun (*masdar*) emphasizing what precedes it, for recitation is a kind of remembrance. Furthermore, if these attributes are applied to all of them, then their conjunction with *fa* (then) indicates their ordering in excellence: either the excellence of the ranks, then of the restraining, then of the recitation, or the reverse. If each of them is applied to specific groups, then it indicates the ordering of the described in the degrees of excellence, meaning that the groups of those who arrange in ranks have excellence, the restrainers are more excellent, and the reciters are more outstanding in excellence, or the reverse.

It was also said: what is meant by those mentioned are the souls of the scholars who act (upon their knowledge): *al-saffat* are their souls arranged in the rows of congregations and their feet in the prayers; *al-zajirat* are those who restrain by admonitions and advice; *al-talIyat* are those who recite the signs of God Most High; *al-darisat* are those who study His laws and rulings.

It was also said: [they are] groups of warriors: *al-saffat* are those who arrange themselves in the places of battle as if they were a solid structure (cf. ﴿كَأنَّهم بُنْيانٌ مَرْصُوصٌ﴾, "as if they were a solidly built structure"), or groups of their commanders who arrange them there; *al-zajirat* are the horses driven for jihad, and the enemy in the battlefields by repulsion; *al-talIyat* are the signs of God Most High, His remembrance and His glorification, within these [actions]. The discussion of the conjunction and its indication of the ordering of the attributes in excellence, or the ordering of what they describe in it, is as previously mentioned. As for the indication of ordering in existence, as in the words of the poet:

"Alas for Zabbana, for the one who attacks at dawn, then the one who takes the spoil, then the one who returns."

it is not apparent in any of the mentioned groups, for even if the precedence of the rows over the restraining is granted among the angels and the warriors, the lateness of recitation after the restraining is not apparent.

It was also said: *al-saffat* are the birds, from the words of God Most High: ﴿والطَّيْرُ صافّاتٍ﴾ ("and the birds in flight"); *al-zajirat* are everything that restrains from sins; *al-talIyat* are everyone who recites the Book of God Most High. It was also said: *al-zajirat* are the Qur'anic calamities (*al-qawari'* al-qur'aniyya). It was read with the assimilation of the *ta'* into the *sad*, the *zay* and the *dhal*.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, your God is One.﴾ It is the answer to the oath (jawab al-qasam), and the sentence serves to affirm the truth, which is monotheism (tawhid), by means of the emphasis through oath that is customary in their speech, and as a preparation for the proof that follows it and speaks to it, namely His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 5:

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and Lord of the easts.﴾ Their existence and their orderly arrangement in this wondrous pattern is among the clearest proofs of the existence of the Maker (al-Sani'), of His knowledge and His power, and the most just evidence of His oneness, as has passed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted.﴾ And "Lord" (rabb) is a second predicate of "inna" (indeed), or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: Owner of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them of existing things, and their Nourisher (murabbi) and the One who brings them to their perfections. By "the easts" (al-mashariq) is meant the rising-points of the sun. The repetition of "Lord" here is for the sake of making the manifestations of lordship (rububiyya) clearly apparent in them and renewed every day, for there are three hundred and sixty easts; the sun rises each day from one of them, and the wests (al-maghareb) vary according to them, and the sun sets each day in one of them. As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾, these are the two easts and the two wests of summer and winter.

﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven﴾, that is, the one nearest to you, ﴿with an adornment﴾, wondrous and marvelous, ﴿the stars﴾. Here ﴿al-kawakib﴾ (الكَواكِبِ) is in the genitive case (بِالجَرِّ) as a substitute (badal) for (zinatin, زِينَةٍ), on the understanding that the word denotes the thing (al-ism), that is, that with which something is adorned, not the verbal noun (al-masdar). For the stars themselves, and the arrangement of some of them relative to others, are an adornment, and what an adornment they are.

It is also read with the construct (idafah), in which case the genitive is explanatory (bayaniyyah), because the word "adornment" is vague and applies to anything with which something is adorned, so the stars come as an explanation of it. It is also permissible that by "the adornment of the stars" is meant that with which they themselves are adorned, namely their light.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "the adornment of the stars" means "the light of the stars."

Furthermore, if (zinah) is taken as a verbal noun, the meaning is as follows: on the supposition that it is construed with the agent, meaning that the stars adorned the heaven, and its original form is "bi-zinati al-kawakib"; and on the supposition that it is construed with the object, meaning that Allah adorned the stars and made them beautiful, and its original form is likewise "bi-zinati al-kawakib." The intended meaning is adornment in the eyes of the beholder (fi ra'y al-'ayn), for all the stars, both the fixed stars (al-thawabit) and the wandering planets (al-sayyarat), appear to onlookers like shining jewels on the surface of the nearest heaven, in wondrous forms and marvelous shapes. This is not undermined by the view that the fixed stars are fixed in the eighth sphere (al-falak al-thamin), and that all except the Moon are in the six intermediate spheres (al-sittah al-mutawassitah), if that is established.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 7:

﴿And as a guard﴾ is in the accusative, either by its being coordinated with "adornment" in terms of meaning, as if it were said: "We created the stars as an adornment for the heaven and as a guard ﴿against every rebellious devil﴾," i.e., one who has departed from obedience, by the hurling of meteors; or by supposing a verb to be implied; or by supposing a verb placed later, which it is the cause of, as if it were said: "And as a guard against every rebellious devil, We adorned it with the stars," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and made them missiles against the devils﴾.

And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 8:

﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly﴾ is a new sentence, brought to explain their condition after the explanation of the guarding of the heaven against them, together with drawing attention to the manner of the guarding and the punishment that befalls them during it. It is not possible to make it a qualifier of (every devil), nor an answer to a presumed question, because the meaning would not be sound; nor a cause of the guarding, on the basis that the original is "so that they do not listen," with the lam deleted as it is deleted in your saying: "I came to you that you might honour me," so that "that they not listen" remains; then with the deletion of "an" (that) and the nullifying of its governance, as in the saying of the one who said:

Ala ayyuhadha al-zajiri ahdura al-waghā
(Is it not so, O one who rebukes me, that I should attend the battle?)

This is because each of these two deletions, taken on its own, is not objectionable; but their combination is among the most objectionable things, from which the sanctuary of the glorious revelation must be purified. The original of (yassammaʿūna) is (yatasammaʿūna), and al-malaʾ al-aʿlā (the exalted assembly) are the angels.

And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, they are the scribes; and from him, the noble angels, upon them be prayer and peace. That is: they do not seek to hear or to listen to them. It has also been read (yasmaʿūna) with the lightened form. ﴿And they are pelted﴾ — they are struck — ﴿from every side﴾ — from all directions of the heaven — when they intend to ascend to it.

﴿Duhuran﴾ is a causal object (ʿillah) of "qadhf" (casting), meaning, for the sake of driving away (al-duhur). Alternatively, it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a state-describing accusative) in the sense of "driven away" (madhḥūrīn), or a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing its verb, since both come from the same root. It has also been read as "daḥūran" with a fatḥah on the dal, meaning a casting that drives away with great force. It is also permitted that it be a verbal noun of the pattern of "qabūl" (acceptance) and "walūʿ" (eagerness). ﴿And for them is a perpetual punishment﴾: that is, for them in the Hereafter, beyond what they suffer in this world from being pelted with shooting stars, is a severe, lasting punishment that does not end. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 10:

﴿Except one who snatches a fragment﴾ It is an exception from the waw of "yastami'un" (they listen), and "man" (one who) is a substitute (badal) for it. "Al-khatf" (snatching) is al-ikhtilas (stealing away), and what is meant is stealing away the speech of the angels by stealth, as the definite form of "al-khatfah" (the fragment) indicates. It is also read with a kasra on the kha' and a shadda-ed ta', and with a fatha on the kha' and a kasra on the ta' with shadda. Their origin is "ikhtataf" (﴿fa-atba'ahu shihabun﴾) meaning: he followed him and overtook him. It is also read "fa-attaba'ahu." "Al-shihab" (the meteor) is what is seen falling swiftly from the sky ﴿piercing⁠﴾, meaning extremely bright, as if it pierces the air with its light. Shayatin are pelted with it when they ascend to eavesdrop, and so it kills them, burns them, or stuns them. They said: whoever of them survives, being alive, returns only out of hope for safety and attaining his aim, like the rider of a ship.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 11:

﴿So ask them﴾ — i.e., seek information from the polytheists of Makkah, ﴿are they stronger in creation, or those whom We have created?﴾ — i.e., more powerful in their makeup and firmer in their structure; or, more difficult to create and harder to bring into being. ﴿Or those whom We have created﴾ — from the angels, the heaven, the earth, what lies between them, the easts, the stars, and the piercing meteors. The word ﴿مَن﴾ (man, "those who") is used to give precedence to rational beings over others, and this is indicated by its unrestricted application and its coming after that, especially the reading of one who read (أمْ مَن عَدَدْنا) ("or those whom We have counted").

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We created them from sticky clay﴾, it is what distinguishes them from the rest of creation, not what distinguishes them from the peoples before them such as ʿAd and Thamud. Also, because the purpose is to establish the Return and to refute their claim of its impossibility, the matter concerning it is the same whether in reference to them or to those before them. It was also read as (لازِمٍ) (lāzimin) and (لاتِبٍ) (lātibin).

﴿Rather, you wonder﴾, i.e., at the power of God Most High over these great creations, and at their denial of the Resurrection, ﴿and they mock﴾ your wonder and your affirmation of the Resurrection. It is also read with a ḍamma on the tā' (تَعْجَبُ, "you wonder" in the first person as a report from God: عَجِبْتُ, "I wonder"), meaning that the perfection of My power and the abundance of My creatures reached such a point that I wonder at them, while these people, out of their ignorance, mock them. Or (the meaning is): I wonder that they deny the Resurrection, though their deeds are such as these, and mock the one who affirms it. Wonder attributed to God Most High is either by way of supposition and imagination (al-far' wa-al-takhyīl), or in the sense of the magnification (al-isti'ẓām) that necessarily accompanies it, for it is a astonishment that seizes a person when he magnifies something. It has also been said that it is implied by a verb of saying, i.e., "Say, O Muhammad: Rather, I wonder."

And when they are reminded, they do not take heed. That is: their constant habit is that when they are admonished with any of the admonitions, ﴿they do not remember﴾, meaning they do not heed. And when there is mentioned to them what indicates the soundness of the resurrection, they do not benefit from it, due to the extreme of their dullness and the deficiency of their reasoning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 14:

﴿And when they see a sign﴾, that is, a miracle indicating the truthfulness of the one who brings it, ﴿they mock﴾ (yastaskhirun), that is, they exaggerate in ridicule, and they say: "It is nothing but magic," or some of them summon others to mock it.

Translation:

﴿And they say: "This is nothing but﴾ — that is, what they see of the dazzling signs — ﴿evident magic.﴾" — clear in its being magic.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 16:

﴿Will we indeed, when we have died and become dust and bones,﴾ meaning: some of our parts were dust and some of them were bones. The dust is mentioned first because it is what the parts that are visible turn into. The governing element of "idha" (when) is what is indicated by "mab'uthun" (resurrected) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Are we indeed to be resurrected?﴾ That is, we will be raised, not the mere fact of being dead itself, because beyond it there are calamities, any one of which alone would suffice as an obstacle. The fronting of the adverbial phrase serves to strengthen the denial of resurrection by directing it to a state that is utterly incompatible with it. Likewise, the repetition of the hamza in "a-inna" (is it indeed that we) is for emphasis and intensification in this matter. Likewise, the adornment of the sentence with "inna" (indeed) and the lam (emphatic particle) is to affirm the denial, not the denial of the affirmation as the outward form of the noble wording might suggest. The fronting of the hamza (interrogative particle) is because it requires initial position, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ according to the view of the majority, since its meaning for them is the denial following upon the matter, not the denial of the following, as is well known. It has also been read with the first hamza omitted, and with only the second hamza omitted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 17:

﴿Or our forefathers of old?﴾ It is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted according to Sibawayh (the early grammarian and author of the Kitab), meaning: "And our forefathers of old too are being resurrected." It has also been said that it is conjoined (ʿatf) to the place (mahall) of inna and its subject, and it has been said that it is conjoined to the pronoun in "mab'uthun" (being resurrected), with the separation provided by the interrogative hamza of denial, which functions like the particle of negation in His exalted saying: ﴿We did not associate partners, nor did our forefathers﴾. Whichever of these it is, their intention is to add to the sense of improbability, on the basis that they are more ancient, so their resurrection is even more remote in their assumption. It is also read: (ʾaw ābāʾunā, "or our forefathers").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 18:

﴿Say﴾ as a rebuke to them, ﴿Yes﴾. The address in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and you will be humbled﴾, is directed at them and at their forefathers by way of taghlib (the grammatical device of giving precedence to the masculine plural or the present company over others, i.e., addressing the group together). The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the subject implied by "نَعَمْ" (yes), meaning: all of you will be resurrected, while the state you are in is that you will be abased and humiliated. It was also read as (نَعِمْ) with a kasra on the ʿayn, and this is a dialect (lughah, a regional variant of Arabic) of the word.

Verse 19 of surah 37: ﴿Then it will be but a single shout﴾. It is either an ambiguous pronoun (ḍamīr mubham) whose explanation is its predicate, or the pronoun referring to the resurrection (al-ba'tha), and the clause is the answer to an implied condition (jawab shart muḍmar), or a justification (ta'līl) for an implied prohibition (nahy muqaddar), meaning: "If that is so, then it is but ..." etc., or "Do not find it difficult, for it is but ..." etc. The zajra (shout) is the cry from zajara (to drive away), as a shepherd drives his sheep when he shouts at them; it is the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya). ﴿Then behold, they﴾ are standing up from their resting places, alive ﴿looking﴾, seeing as they were, or awaiting what will be done to them.

"And they will say": that is, those who are resurrected. The past tense form is used to indicate certainty and settledness. "Woe to us!" meaning: our destruction. "Be present, for this is the time of your presence." His saying, exalted is He, "This is the Day of Judgment" is a justification for their calling out "woe," by way of a resumptive statement; that is: the day on which we will be recompensed for our deeds. They knew this because in the world they used to hear that they would be resurrected, called to account, and recompensed for their deeds. So when they witnessed the resurrection, they became certain of what comes after it as well.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 21:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is the Day of Judgment (al-Fasl) which you used to deny.﴾

﴿This is the Day of Judgment (al-Fasl) which you used to deny.﴾ It is the speech of the angels, answering them by way of rebuke and reproach. It has also been said that it is likewise the speech of some of them to others, and al-Fasl means the judgment (al-qada'), or the separation between the groups of guidance and the groups of misguidance.

And His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 22:

﴿Gather those who did wrong﴾ — an address from Allah, exalted and majestic is He, to the angels, or from some of them to others, to gather the wrongdoers from their station to the place of standing (al-mawqif). It has also been said: from the place of standing to Hell (al-Jahim). ﴿And their spouses﴾ — that is, their counterparts and peers among the disobedient, the worshipper of idols together with its worshippers, and the worshipper of the stars together with its worshippers, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you were three kinds of spouses﴾ [Qur'an 56:7]. It has also been said: their companions among the devils. It has also been said: their wives who were upon their religion. ﴿And what they used to worship﴾.

"﴿min dūni llāh﴾ (besides Allah): from among the idols and the like, as an added cause of their regret and humiliation. It has been said: it is general but specified by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the good reward has preceded from Us﴾, the noble verse. You should know that the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) refers only to the polytheists, and it was brought in to give the reason for the ruling by what is in the scope of its clause (ṣilah). So there is neither generality nor specification. ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾: that is, make known to them its way and direct them toward it. And in it there is mockery of them."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 24:

﴿And stop them﴾: detain them at the place of standing (al-mawqif), for it is as if the angels hastened to do what they were commanded regarding their gathering to Hellfire, and so they were ordered to do this. It is given as the reason by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, they are to be questioned﴾, as a notice from the very beginning that this is not for pardoning them, nor so that they may rest by delaying the punishment altogether, but so that they may be questioned. However, not about their beliefs and deeds, as has been said, for that has already taken place before they were ordered to Hellfire; rather, it is about what His saying, may He be exalted, expresses:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 25:

﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?﴾ This is in the manner of rebuke, reproach and mockery; that is, none of you helps another, as you used to claim in the world. The postponing of this question until that time is because it is the time of the descent of punishment, of the utmost need for help, and of the state in which hope of it is completely cut off. Thus rebuke and reproach at that time are far more striking in effect and influence. It has also been read as ﴿لا تَتَناصَرُونَ﴾ and ﴿لا تَنّاصَرُونَ﴾ with idgham (assimilation of the two consonants).

Quran verse: ﴿Nay, on that Day they will be in full submission.﴾

Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim): "Submitting" means they are compliant and humbled, because their helplessness has become evident and every avenue of stratagem has been closed to them. Or, it means that some of them surrendered to others and abandoned them out of helplessness, so all of them are submitting, none of them gaining victory.

"And they [will] turn to one another" (﴿وَأقْبَلَ بَعْضُهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾) at that time. They are the followers and the leaders, or the disbelievers and their companions (in misguidance), "questioning one another" (﴿يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾): some of them ask others a questioning of reproach, in the manner of contention and dispute.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 28:

﴿They will say﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), coming as an answer to a question that arises from the narration of their mutual questioning, as if it were said: "How did they question one another?" So it is said: "They will say"—that is, the followers to the leaders, or all of them to their companions (qurana'): ﴿Indeed, you used to come to us﴾ in the world ﴿from the right (ʿan al-yamin)﴾—from the strongest and most powerful directions; or from the religion; or from the good; as if you were benefiting us the way the bird of omen (al-sanih) benefits, so we followed you and perished. It is a metaphor taken from the right hand of a human being, which is the more noble, stronger and more beneficial of the two sides; for this reason it was called "yamin," and one seeks good omen from the sanih. Or [it means] from force and compulsion, so that you compelled us to error (al-ghayy), and this is the most fitting to the answer. Or [it means] from oaths, since they used to swear that they were upon the truth.

(p-189) ﴿Qālū﴾ (they say) is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), as before. That is: the leaders or the companions said: ﴿Nay, you were not believers.﴾ That is: We did not prevent you from faith; rather, you did not believe by your own choosing, and you turned away from it while you were able to attain it, and you preferred disbelief over it.

Surah 37, verse 30 in Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim):

﴿And we had no authority over you﴾ — that is, no compulsion or domination by which we would strip you of your free choice, ﴿but you were a people who were rebellious (ṭāghīn)﴾ — choosing transgression of your own accord and persisting in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 31:

﴿So the word of our Lord has come due against us﴾, i.e., it became binding upon us and was confirmed against us, ﴿that we will surely taste [the punishment]﴾, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you of them, all together﴾. ﴿Indeed, we are the ones who will taste﴾, i.e., the punishment that the threat was given of.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 32:

﴿So We led you astray, for we ourselves were astray﴾ — We called you to error with a call that did not compel you, and you responded to us by your own choice and your preference for error over guidance. ﴿Indeed, we were astray﴾ — so there is no blame upon us for our approaching you to lead you astray with that degree of calling, so that you would become like us in error.

Translation of the passage:

﴿Indeed they﴾, that is, the followers and those they followed, ﴿on that Day, in the punishment, will be sharers﴾, just as they were sharers in misguidance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 34:

﴿Indeed, thus⁠﴾ meaning: like that wondrous act which the legislative wisdom (al-hikmah al-tashri'iyyah) requires, ﴿We deal with the criminals⁠﴾ those who go to extremes in criminality, and they are the polytheists (al-mushrikun), as is indicated by the causal clause introduced by His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 35:

﴿Indeed, they, when it was said to them﴾ by way of invitation and instruction, ﴿"There is no deity except Allah"﴾ [they] ﴿were arrogant﴾ toward accepting it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verses 36–37:

﴿And they say, "Shall we really abandon our gods for a mad poet?"﴾ ﴿Nay, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers.﴾ This is a rejection of them and a refutation of their claim, by making clear that what he brought of monotheism (tawhid) is the truth, which proof has established and on which all the messengers – upon them be prayer and peace – have agreed. So where are poetry and madness from his lofty sanctuary?!

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verses 36–37:

﴿And they say, "Shall we really abandon our gods for a mad poet?"﴾ ﴿Nay, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers.﴾ This is a rejection of them and a refutation of their claim, by making clear that what he brought of monotheism (tawhid) is the truth, which proof has established and on which all the messengers – upon them be prayer and peace – have agreed. So where are poetry and madness from his lofty sanctuary?!

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 38:

﴿Indeed, you﴾ (for what you did of associating partners with God, denying the Messenger (ﷺ), and arrogance) ﴿will surely taste the painful punishment﴾. The shift from address to the third person (iltifat) serves to show the full extent of anger against them. It was also read with the accusative "al-'adhab" (the punishment) on the basis of an assumed deletion of the nun (in lidha'iqu, "those who taste"), as in his saying:

*wa-la dhakiru Allahi illa qaliluan*

And it was also read "la-dha'iqun al-'adhab" (with the nun retained), in accordance with the original form.
﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾. That is: "except the recompense for what you used to do of evil deeds," or "except with what you used to do of them."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 40:

﴿Except the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ This is an exceptive phrase of disconnection (istithna' munqati') from the pronoun in "dhA'iqu" (taste), and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD), introduced in haste to establish the truth by clarifying that their tasting of the punishment comes only from their own side and not from the side of anyone else at all. As for making it an exception from the pronoun in "tujzawn" (you will be recompensed), in the sense that the disbelievers are recompensed only according to the measure of their deeds, while the chosen servants of Allah are recompensed with multiplied increases, this has no basis at all, especially making it a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) with the generalization of the address in "tujzawn" to all those under obligation, for that is not even within the realm of possibility. So the meaning is: indeed you are tasting the painful punishment, but the chosen servants of Allah, the monotheists, are not like that.

And His Exalted saying:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to them, indicating that they are set apart, by their sincerity in worshipping God Most High to the exclusion of all others, with a far-reaching distinction. Through this they are arranged in the line of observed things. The sense of distance it carries, together with the closeness of time of the one indicated, signals the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence. The demonstrative is the subject (mubtada’, the topic of the nominal sentence). God's statement, Most High: ﴿for them﴾ is either its predicate (khabar), and His statement, Most High: ﴿a provision﴾ is raised as the agent (fa‘iliyya, the doer) by virtue of the sense of being established (istiqrar) contained in the preposition "lahum" (لَهُمْ). Or, the demonstrative is the subject, "lahum" (لَهُمْ) is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and the whole clause is the predicate of "ulā’ika" (أُولَئِكَ). The major clause is a resumptive sentence (isti’nāf) that explains in detail what the exception (istithnā’) had stated in general terms. It was also said that it is the predicate of a disjunctive exception (istithnā’ munqati‘), on the basis that it is construed as a subject (mu’awwal bil-mubtada’). God's statement, Most High: ﴿known﴾ means: known in its qualities, such as beauty of appearance, sweetness of taste, fragrance of scent, and similar attributes of perfection. It was also said that it means known in its time, as in God's statement, Most High: ﴿And they will have their provision therein, morning and evening﴾ (Q. 19:62). And God's statement, Most High:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 42:

﴿Fawakih﴾ (fruits) is either a substitute (badal) for (rizq, provision), or the predicate of an implied subject, i.e., "that provision is fruits." Its being singled out for mention is because all the provisions of the people of Paradise are fruits, that is, what is eaten merely for pleasure (al-talaqqudh) and not for sustenance (al-iqtiyat), because they are free of need for staple food, their creation being perfected and preserved from the dissolution that necessitates replacement (al-badal).

It is said: it is because fruits are followers (atba') of all other foods, so mentioning them suffices in place of mentioning them. ﴿And they will be honored﴾ with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, such that no humiliation will touch them; and that is the greatest of rewards and the most fitting for people of high aspirations. It is also said: they are honored in attaining it, in that it reaches them without toil or asking, as is the nature of the provisions of this world. It has also been read as (mukarramun) with the doubled letter (tashdid).

﴿In gardens of bliss﴾, that is, in gardens containing nothing but bliss. It is either an adverbial of place or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the implicit pronoun in (mukramūn, "honoured"), or a second predicate (khabar) for "ulā'ika" ("those").

(p-191) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Upon couches, facing one another﴾

﴿Upon couches﴾ may be taken as a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah) or as a predicate (khabariyyah). Accordingly, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿facing one another﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the pronoun concealed within it (al-mustakinn fīhi), or of ﴿honored﴾ (mukramūn), and His saying, exalted is He:

Yutaf 'alayhim: "They are served" — let me translate the passage.

﴿They are served﴾ — either it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the narration of the concealed (i.e., hidden from view) gatherings of their companionship; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿reclining face to face﴾, or from one of the two prepositional phrases. It has also been permitted that it is a qualifying clause (sifah) for ﴿honored﴾.

﴿with a cup﴾ — meaning, with a vessel containing wine, or with wine itself; for the cup (ka's) is used to refer to the wine itself, as in the words of the one who said:

"And a cup I drank for pleasure, and another I was treated with from it."

﴿from a flowing spring﴾ — this is connected to an implied element that serves as a qualifier of "cup": that is, "originating from a flowing drink," or "from a flowing spring" (ma'in), which is that which runs over the surface of the earth and is visible to the eyes, or that which emerges from the springs, from "'ana al-ma'u" when water gushes forth. The adjective is applied to wine, though it belongs to water, because it flows in Paradise in rivers as water flows. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And rivers of wine﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 46:

﴿Bayḍāʾ, delicious to those who drink.﴾ These are also two attributes of (kaʾs, a cup). Describing it as (ladhdhah, delicious) is either for emphasis, as if it were the very essence of delight, or because it is the feminine of (al-ladhdh, meaning al-ladhīdh, the delicious), whose pattern is (fa'l). He said:

؎ And a sweet sleep, like the taste of the Ṣarkhadī (wine), I left it in the land of enemies out of fear of misfortunes.

He means by it sleep.

ﷺ-less passage; translate faithfully.

**﴿There is no harm in it [lā fīhā ghawl]﴾**: i.e., no ghā'ila (harmful effect), as in the wine of this world, from ghālahu, meaning he corrupted him and destroyed him; and from this comes the ghūl (ghoul, a destructive demon). **﴿Nor are they made drunk by it [wa-lā hum ʿanhā yunzafūn]﴾**: i.e., they do not become intoxicated. It is from nazafa al-shārib, so he is nazīf and manzūf, when his intellect has gone; and it is said of one who has been stabbed: nazafa, then died, when all his blood has come out. This was singled out for negation, although it is included in what precedes it of negating ghawl from it, because it is among the greatest corruptions of wine, as if it were a genus in its own right. The meaning: there is in it no kind of corruption, neither colic, nor headache, nor hangover, nor raving, nor idle talk, nor sinfulness; and nor are they intoxicated.

It is also recited as (yunzifūn) with a kasra on the zāy, from anzafa al-shārib, when his intellect or his drink is exhausted; and it is recited as (yanzufūn) with a ḍamma on the zāy, from nazufa yanzufu, with a ḍamma on the zāy in both.

And with them are those restraining their glances, [who] have restricted their eyes to their husbands, not casting their gaze toward others. ﴿Wide-eyed, lovely-eyed﴾ — large-eyed (nujl al-‘uyun), plural of ‘ayna’ (a woman with large, beautiful eyes); al-najal is the breadth of the eye.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 49:

﴿As if they were eggs, well-guarded.﴾ They are likened to ostrich eggs kept safe from dust and the like, in their clearness and whiteness mixed with a slight yellowness, for that is the most beautiful of the colours of bodies.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 50:

﴿Then some of them will turn to others, questioning one another.﴾ It is coordinated with (yutaf, "is passed around") — i.e., they drink and converse over the wine, as is the custom of drinking. He said:

؎ Nothing remains of the pleasures except the conversations of the noble over the wine

So some of them turn to others, questioning one another about virtues and knowledge, and about what befell them and what befell them against them in the world. The expression of it in the past tense (fa'a'bala, "then turned") is for emphasis and to indicate that its occurrence is certain and decreed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 51:

﴿قالَ قائِلٌ مِنهُمْ﴾ amid their exchanges of speech ﴿إنِّي كانَ لِي﴾ in the world ﴿قَرِينٌ﴾ a companion, one who kept company with me.

﴿He says﴾ to me, in the manner of rebuke, about the faith and belief in the resurrection (al-ba'th) that I used to hold: ﴿Are you truly among those who affirm (al-musaddiqin)?﴾ That is, affirming the resurrection. It was also recited with the ṣād (ص) doubled (شدّ الصّاد), from taṣaddaq (تَصَدَّقَ). The first reading is more suitable to His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 53:

﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be recompensed?﴾ That is: shall we indeed be resurrected and requited? It is from al-din (debt, here meaning recompense), or it means: shall we indeed be governed? One says: "dana-hu," meaning "sasa-hu" (he governed him, he managed him), and from this comes the hadith: "The wise one is he who subjects (dana) his soul."

It is also said: A man gave away his wealth seeking the Face of Allah, Exalted is He, then he came to need, and he asked some of his brethren for help. He said: "Where is your wealth?" He replied: "I gave it in charity, so that Allah, Exalted is He, would compensate me in the Hereafter with something better than it." He said: "Are you then one of those who believe in the Day of Religion (the Day of Judgment), or one of those who give charity seeking reward? By Allah, I will not give you anything." Thus the mention here of their death and of their becoming dust and bones is, in that case, for emphasizing the denial of recompense, which is founded upon the denial of resurrection.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 37, verse 54:

﴿Qala﴾ (He said): that is, that speaker, after he had recounted to his companions the statement of his associate in the world. ﴿Hal antum muttali'un﴾ ("Would you like to look down?"): that is, upon the people of the Fire, so that I may show you that associate. He intends by this to demonstrate the truthfulness of what he related.

It has also been said: the speaker is Allah, Exalted, or some of the angels, who say to them: "Would you like to look down upon the people of the Fire, so that I may show you that associate, and you may know where your station is relative to theirs?" It has been said: indeed, in Paradise there are openings (kuwan, sing. kuwwa, "apertures") through which its people look down upon the people of the Fire.

﴿Then he looked down﴾, that is, upon them, ﴿and saw him﴾, that is, his companion, ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾, that is, in its middle. It is also read (fa-aṭṭali‘a), in the present subjunctive form, and it is read (muṭli‘ūna) [as in "Are you looking down?"], and (fa-aṭla‘a and fa-ṭla‘a) with the light (takhfīf) pronunciation, following the form of the past tense and the subjunctive present. It is said: ṭala‘a ‘alaynā fulān, iṭṭala‘a and aṭla‘a have one meaning: someone looked down on us. The meaning is: "Are you (all) looking down at the companion? Then I too will look down," or he was offered the looking down, and they accepted what he offered, so he then looked down. If iṭṭilā‘ (looking down) is taken as transitive, the meaning is that when he made their looking down a condition of his own looking down, as is the custom of companions, it was as though they were the ones who made him look down.

It is said: the address in this reading is to the angels. It is also read (muṭli‘ūnī) with a kasra on the nūn, meaning muṭli‘ūna iyyāya (you are making me look down), so he placed the attached pronoun in place of the detached one, as in their saying:

hum al-fā‘ilūna al-khayra wal-āmirūnah

or the active participle was likened to the present tense because of the affinity between them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 56:

﴿He said﴾ i.e., the speaker, addressing his companion: ﴿By God, you almost ruined me, indeed you nearly brought me to destruction﴾ i.e., you were about to destroy me through seduction. It is also read (لَتُغْوِينِ) "you would have led me astray" (p-193), and the tā' in it carries the sense of wonder (ta'ajjub). And inna here is the lightened (mukhaffafah) form of inna, its ism being the omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the lam is the lam of distinction (lam al-fāriqah), i.e., "By God, indeed the matter is that you nearly ruined me, you were about to lead me to destruction."

**Qur'anic quotation:** ﴿Had it not been for the grace of my Lord﴾ — by guidance and protection — ﴿I would surely have been among those brought forward﴾; that is, among those who were brought to the punishment, just as you and your like have been brought to it.

And His, exalted is He, saying:

Verse 58: ﴿Are we not going to die,﴾ a return to the conversation of his companions after completing the speech with his fellow, out of exultation and joy at the great bounty and everlasting bliss that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has granted them. The hamza (alif of interrogation, used for affirmation) carries here the sense of wonder, and the fa' (fa of conjunction) is coordinated with an implied element required by the composition of the speech, meaning: "Are we not made eternal and pampered, so that we are not dying?" That is, not among those whose nature is death. It is also read: (bi-ma'itin, "not dying" in the sense of "not dead").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 59:

﴿Except our first death﴾, the one that occurred in the world, and it encompasses what is in the grave after being brought to life for questioning. He said this in confirmation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾. It has also been said: when the people of Paradise first enter Paradise, they do not know that they will not die. Then death is brought in the form of a horned ram, white with black markings, and it is slaughtered, and it is called out: "O people of Paradise, eternity, there is no death! O people of the Fire, eternity, there is no death!" They know it, and so they say that, speaking of the blessing of God, exalted is He, and rejoicing in it. ﴿And we will not be punished﴾, as the disbelievers are, for deliverance from punishment is also a magnificent blessing that warrants speaking of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 60:

﴿Indeed, this﴾, i.e., the great matter in which we are, ﴿is truly the great triumph﴾. It was also said that this is from the words of Allah, may He be exalted and glorified, confirming their statement and affirming it. It was recited as (Indeed, this is the great provision) (lahuwa al-rizq al-azim), meaning what they were provided with of the supreme happiness.

For the attainment of such a thing, let those who labor labor. That is: for the attainment of this exalted goal, those who strive must labor, not for the swiftly passing worldly pleasures that are mixed with all kinds of pain. And this also may be from the words of the Lord of Might.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 62:

﴿Is that better as a welcome (nuzul), or the tree of al-Zaqqum?﴾ The root meaning of nuzul (a welcome gift, provision for a guest) is surplus and gain, so it was borrowed to refer to what results from a thing. Its accusative position is then that of a specification (tamyiz), meaning: Is that known provision, whose outcome is pleasure and joy, better as a welcome, or the tree of al-Zaqqum, whose outcome is pain and grief?! It is also said that nuzul is what is prepared and made ready of food for the arriving guest, so its accusative position is that of a circumstantial state (hal). The meaning is that the known provision is the welcome of the people of Paradise, while the welcome of the people of Hellfire is the tree of al-Zaqqum. So which of the two is better in being a welcome?! Al-Zaqqum is the name of a tree with small leaves, foul-smelling, bitter, and of a disagreeable odor, which grows in Tihama; the described tree was named after it.(p-194)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 63:

﴿Indeed, We made it a trial for the wrongdoers.﴾ A trial (miḥnah) and a punishment for them in the Hereafter, and a test (ibtila') for them in this world. For when they heard that it (the tree) is in the Fire, they said: "How is that possible, when the Fire burns trees?!" They did not know that He who is able to create an animal that lives in the Fire and takes pleasure in it is even more able to create a tree in the Fire and preserve it from being burned.

﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs forth from the root of the Blazing Fire.﴾ Its growing place is at the bottom of Jahannam (Hell), and its branches rise up to its levels (darakat). It is also recited as: نابِتَةٌ في أصْلِ الجحيم (nābitatun fī aṣli al-jaḥīm), where the word nābitatun, meaning "growing," replaces takhruju, meaning "comes out," so the sense is "a tree growing at the root of the Blazing Fire."

Its spathe (ṭalʿuhā): that is, its fruit-bearing cluster which emerges from it. It is used metaphorically from the spathe (ṭalʿ) of the date palm, because it shares with it in shape and in emerging from the tree. They said: the first of the dates is ṭalʿ, then khilāl, then balaḥ, then busr, then ruṭab, then tamr. ﴿As though it were the heads of devils﴾ in extreme ugliness and horror. This is a comparison with the imagined, like the comparison of one surpassing in beauty to an angel. It was also said: the devils (shayāṭīn) are the terrifying serpents, hideous in appearance, which have crests. It was also said: there is a tree called al-Astunn (the euphorbia), rough, foul-smelling, bitter, of repulsive form, whose fruit is called (the heads of devils).

﴿Indeed, they will be eating from it﴾: that is, from the tree, or from its spathe (ṭalʿ), so the feminine gender is borrowed from the noun it is annexed to (al-muḍāf ilayhi). ﴿And filling their bellies from it﴾: because hunger is overpowering, or because they are compelled to eat it, even though they dislike it, so that this becomes a gate of punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 67:

﴿Then indeed for them thereafter﴾ upon the tree from which they filled their bellies after they had eaten their fill of it, and thirst overcame them, and their requests for drink grew long, as the word "thumma" (then) indicates. It is also possible that it [the "then"] is for the increased loathsomeness and foulness of their drink. ﴿a mixture of boiling water﴾: a drink of ghassaq (a cold, putrid discharge) or pus, mixed with scalding water that cuts up their intestines. It is also read with a damma (lashawban, with the first letter vowelled with u), and it is the name of what is mixed in, while the first reading is a verbal noun (masdar) that was used as a name.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 68:

﴿Then indeed their return﴾ means their destination (maṣīr). It has also been read thus: ﴿surely to the Blazing Fire (al-Jaḥīm)﴾, meaning to its ranks (darakāt), or to the Fire itself. For the zaqqūm and the ḥamīm are a provision (nuzul) presented to them before they enter it. It was also said: the ḥamīm is outside of it, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿This is Hell which the guilty used to deny﴾ ﴿They will go around between it and boiling, scalding water﴾. They are taken away from their stations and dwellings in the Fire to the tree of zaqqūm, and they eat from it until they become full; then they are given to drink from the ḥamīm; then they are returned to the Fire. This is supported by the reading (thumma inna munqalabahum), ﴿then indeed their return﴾ being read as their overturning (munqalab).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 69:

﴿Indeed, they found their fathers astray.﴾ This is a statement of the reason for their deserving the various kinds of punishment that were mentioned, namely their blind imitation of their fathers in religion, without them or their fathers possessing anything at all to hold on to. That is, they found them astray in the reality of the matter, having nothing that could serve as a pretext, let alone as valid evidence. (p-195)

Translation:

﴿So they hasten along in their footsteps﴾ without reflecting whether they are upon the truth or not, even though it is evident that they are upon falsehood with the least consideration. Al-ihra' (hastening) is intense haste, as if they are being driven and urged to hurry in following their footsteps. It was also said: it is a hastening in which there is a semblance of trembling.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 71:

﴿And indeed, most of the former peoples went astray before them﴾, that is: before your people, the Quraysh. ﴿Most of the former ones﴾ refers to the earlier nations, and this is the answer to an omitted oath (qasam mahdhuf). Likewise is His, may He be exalted, saying:

And We certainly sent among them warners (﴿مُنْذِرِينَ﴾): that is, prophets of great number and of weighty standing, who made clear to them the falsehood of what they were upon, and warned them of its dire consequence. The repetition of the oath serves to show the full extent of concern in establishing the content of each of the two sentences.

﴿So look how was the outcome of those who were warned﴾ — how terrible and dreadful it was, since they paid no heed to the warning and did not lift up their heads to it. The address is either to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is able to witness their traces. And since the meaning is that they were destroyed with a dreadful destruction, the sincere ones (al-mukhlasun) are excepted from them by His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾. That is: those whom Allah has purified (akhlasahum Allah) by granting them success in faith and in acting upon the requirements of the warning. It is also read as (al-mukhlisin) with a kasra on the lam, meaning: those who made their religion sincere for Allah, exalted is He.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 37, verse 75:**

﴿And Noah certainly called out to Us﴾. This is a detailed account (*tafsil*) of what was summarized earlier, namely the conditions of some of the messengers and the good end they came to. It also includes an account of the bad end of some of those who were warned, as indicated by God's words: ﴿So see how was the end of those who were warned﴾. Among them were the people of Noah, the family of Pharaoh, the people of Lot, and the people of Elias (Ilyas). It also explains the good end of some of those whom God purified and guided to faith, as indicated by the exception (*istithna'*), such as the people of Jonah, peace be upon him. The reason for beginning with the story of Noah before the other stories is clear and needs no explanation. The "lam" is the answer to an omitted oath, and likewise what is in God's words ﴿Then how excellent were the Responders﴾. The meaning is: By God, Noah certainly called upon Us when he despaired of his people's faith, after he had invited them to it for long ages and eras, and his call had only increased them in flight and aversion. So We answered him in the best way. By God, We are indeed the excellent Responders. Thus what was omitted was omitted, relying on what was mentioned as evidence for it. The plural form indicates majesty and grandeur.
And We rescued him and his family from the great distress. [He said:] That is, from the drowning; and it has been said: from the harm of his people.

(p-196) ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾ only, since We destroyed the disbelievers in accordance with his supplication: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth any of the disbelievers a dwelling-dweller﴾. It has been narrated that every one who was with him in the ship died except his sons and their wives; or it means that they are the ones who remained, reproducing until the Day of Resurrection.

Qatadah said: All people are from the descendants of Noah, peace be upon him, and he had three sons: Sam, Ham, and Japheth. Sam is the father of the Arabs, Persians, and Romans; Ham is the father of the Sudanese from the East to the West; and Japheth is the father of the Turks, Yajuj, and Majuj.
The Qur'anic verse: ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾, that is, among the nations.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 79:

﴿Peace be upon Noah﴾. That is: this very statement, and it comes as a quotation (ḥikāyah), like your saying: "I recited (sūrah anzalnāhā)." The meaning is: they greet him with a greeting, and they invoke blessings upon him continually, nation after nation. It was also said: there is an implied speech (qawl muqaddar), that is, "so We said." And it was also said: the verb tarakna (We left) has been made to imply the meaning of qulna (We said).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿among the worlds﴾ is connected to the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa al-majrūr), and its meaning is a supplication for the permanence and continuation of this greeting forever among the worlds, of the angels and the two groups (al-thaqalān), jinn and humankind, all of them.

His saying, exalted is He:

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 80:

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ This is a statement of the reason (ta'lil) for what was done for him, peace be upon him, of the noble honour: the excellent answering of his supplication in the best manner, the continuation of his offspring, the perpetuation of his good remembrance, and the salutation of all the worlds upon him until the end of time, by reason of his being among the company of those known for good-doing and firmly established in it. And that is by way of recompensing good with good. "That" (dhalika) points to the noble honours mentioned which came as a recompense for him, peace be upon him. The sense of distance in it, despite the nearness of the time of what is indicated, serves to signify the loftiness of his rank and the remoteness of his station in excellence and nobility. The kaf (in "thus") is connected to what follows it, i.e.: "Like that complete recompense, We reward those who are complete in good-doing," not a lesser recompense than it.

And His, exalted is He, saying:

Indeed, he was among Our believing servants. This is a reason given for his being among the good-doers (al-muhsinin), by the purity of his servitude and the perfection of his faith. And in it is a clear indication of the greatness of these two qualities, which is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 82:

﴿Then We drowned the others.﴾ That is: those other than Noah and his family, namely the disbelievers of his people, all of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 83:

﴿And indeed, among his followers﴾ means: among those who followed him in the fundamentals of the religion, ﴿was Abraham﴾, even though the subsidiary laws of their two sacred laws (shara'i') differed. It is also permissible that there was a complete or greater agreement between their two laws.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "From the people of his religion and upon his sunnah; or among those who followed him in steadfastness in the religion of Allah, and in enduring the deniers." And there were not between the two of them except two prophets, Hud and Salih, peace be upon them; and between Noah and Abraham there were two thousand six hundred and forty years.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 84:

﴿When he came to his Lord﴾ is in the accusative case, governed by (udhkur, "remember"), or it is connected to what is implied in al-shi'ah (the party/faction) of the meaning of support and following (al-mushaya'ah). ﴿With a sound heart﴾ means: free from the afflictions of the hearts, or from the preoccupying attachments that distract from devoting oneself (al-tabattul) to God, Mighty and Majestic. The meaning of his coming to his Lord with it is his sincerity toward Him, as if he came bringing it as a gift presented to Him, by way of metaphor (tamthil).

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾ It is a substitute (badal) for the first (the preceding "إذ" clause, i.e., "when he came to his Lord with a sound heart"), or it is an adverbial complement (zarf) governing "جاء" (came) or "سليم" (sound), meaning: what is the thing that you worship?

Note on the Arabic terms: badal (substitute, a grammatical apposition replacing an earlier element), zarf (adverb of time or place, here indicating when), and ﴿ماذا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ is parsed as an interrogative "ماذا" functioning as a question about the object of worship.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 86:

﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God, that you desire?﴾ That is: Do you desire gods other than God as a falsehood, i.e., for the sake of falsehood? He placed the object before the verb for emphasis (al-'inaya), then placed the object of purpose (al-maf'ul lahu) before the direct object (al-maf'ul bihi), because the more important matter is confronting them with the fact that they are upon falsehood and vanity in their polytheism. It is also permissible that ﴿ifkan﴾ be a direct object, meaning "Do you desire a falsehood?", and then he explains the falsehood by his saying: ﴿gods other than God﴾, indicating that they are themselves a falsehood, for emphasis (li-l-mubalagha). Or it may be that worshipping them is intended, with the governed noun elided (bi-hadhf al-mudaf). It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial accusative (hal) meaning "lying/fabricating" (afikin).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 87:

﴿So what do you think of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ That is: of the One who is deserving of worship by virtue of being the Lord of the worlds, such that you abandoned worshipping Him alone and associated with Him the most base of His creatures. Or: what do you think of Him? What is He among things, such that you made the idols equals to Him? Or: what do you think of Him? What will He do to you, and how will He punish you after what you did of associating others with Him?

﴿So he glanced a glance at the stars.﴾ It is said: he (peace be upon him) had a fever that came at a fixed time during some hours of the night. So he looked at the stars to know whether that hour had come. Then the fever had indeed come.

﴿So he said, "Indeed, I am sick."﴾ He was truthful in this, and he made it an excuse for not joining them at their festival. It was also said that he meant: "I am sick at heart because of your disbelief." It was also said that he looked into their science, their books, or their rulings. There is nothing preventing this, since his aim, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), was to create the impression among them when they wanted to take him out to their place of worship and leave him behind. These people were astrologers (*najjāmīn*, those who predict by the stars), so he gave them the impression that he had derived from a sign in the stars that he was sick, meaning that he was on the verge of sickness, namely plague, which was the most prevalent of their diseases. They feared contagion, so they would scatter away from him. They fled from him to their place of worship and left him in the house of the idols. This is His saying, exalted is He:

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating﴾

Translation of the commentary:

﴿So they turned away from him, retreating﴾ means: fleeing, for fear of contagion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 91:

﴿Then he turned aside to their gods﴾, that is, he went to them secretly, and its original sense is inclining by means of a stratagem. ﴿Then he said﴾ to the idols, mockingly, ﴿"Will you not eat?"﴾ That is, of the food that they used to prepare beside them so that it would be blessed by them.
{Quranic quotation: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not speak?﴾} That is: [to answer] me.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 93:

﴿فَراغَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ means he turned upon them, inclining over them (fa-mala musta'liyan 'alayhim). His statement, the Exalted: ﴿ضَرْبًا بِاليَمِينِ﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for (raagha 'alayhim), since it carries the meaning of (darabahum, he struck them). Or it is a verbal noun for a hidden verb, which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, meaning: "So he turned upon them, striking them with a strike." Or it is a circumstantial clause from it (the subject), on the basis that it is a verbal noun in the sense of the active participle, meaning: "So he turned upon them, striking with the right hand," that is, a severe and powerful strike. This is because the right hand (al-yamin) is the stronger and more forceful of the two limbs, and the strength of the instrument requires the strength and intensity of the action. It was also said: "with strength and vigor," as in his saying:

"When a banner is raised for his glory, 'Urabah receives it with the right hand."

That is, with strength.

On this basis rests the naming of the oath as "yamin" (right hand), because it strengthens speech and emphasizes it. It was also said: it is named so because of the oath itself, which is His statement, the Exalted: ﴿وَتاللَّهِ لأكِيدَنَّ أصْنامَكُمْ﴾ (By God, I will surely scheme against your idols).

**"They came hastening toward him"**: i.e., those who had been ordered to bring him (peace be upon him), after they had returned from their festival to the house of the idols, found them broken, so they asked about the perpetrator, and they suspected that he (peace be upon him) had done it. So it was said: "Bring him," **"hastening"** is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the waw of *aqbalū* (they came), meaning: they hurry, from the *zafīf* (rapid running) of ostriches. It is also read as *yazifūna* (yazifūn), from *azifa*, meaning he entered into *zafīf*, or from *azaffahu*, meaning he made him run at a *zafīf*, i.e., some of them push others along. *Yuzaffūna* (yuzaffūn), in the passive form, means they are driven at a *zafīf*. *Yazifūna* (yazifūn) is from *wazafa*, *yazifu*, meaning he hastened. *Yuzafūna* (yuzafūn) is from *zafāhu*, meaning he urged him on, as if some of them were urging others on because of their eagerness toward him (peace be upon him).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 95:

﴿Qāla﴾ [He said]: i.e., after they had brought him, peace be upon him, and there had passed between him (ﷺ) and them such exchanges as is expressed by His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿They said: "Did you do this to our gods, O Abraham?"﴾ up to His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"Surely you know that these do not speak."﴾ ﴿"Do you worship what you carve?"﴾ — what you carve of the idols. And His, the Exalted, saying:

﴿Wa-Allahu khalaqakum wa-ma ta'malun﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of (تَعْبُدُونَ) [taʿbudūn], emphasizing the denunciation and rebuke. That is, the situation is that God, Exalted is He, created you and created what you make, for the substances of their idols and their material are by God's creation, and their form, although it is by their action, is by His empowering them to it and His creating what their action depends upon, such as the motives, the tools and the causes. As for (مَا تَعْمَلُونَ) [mā taʿmalūn], it may be a reference to the idols, so it is placed in the position of the pronoun of (مَا تَنْحِتُونَ) [mā tanḥitūn], to indicate that their being created by God, Exalted and Majestic is not only in respect of their carving them, but also in respect of all their other works, such as shaping, decorating, adorning and the like. Or it may be on its general sense, so that it includes the idols in a primary way (p-199), together with what it contains of establishing the truth by explaining that everything they make, whatever it may be, is created by Him, glorified is He. It has also been said that (مَا) [mā] is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning "your work," and it has been said that it carries the sense of the object, and that when their action is by God's creation, the object of their action that depends on their action is more deserving of that.

﴿They said, "Build for him a structure and throw him into the blazing fire."﴾ That is: into the fire that is intensely kindled, from al-juhmah, which is the intensity of blazing. The lam (in al-jahim) is a substitute for the genitive noun that was added to, that is, the blaze of that structure. The manner of their building for him has been mentioned in Surat al-Anbiya' (Surah 21).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 98:

﴿They intended a scheme against him﴾, for when he (ﷺ) overcame them with the argument and silenced them, they pursued what they pursued so that their incapacity would not become evident to the common people. ﴿So We made them the lowest﴾, the most humiliated, by nullifying their scheme and by making it a clear proof of the exalted standing of his (ﷺ) status, through making the fire cool and safe for him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 99:

﴿And he said: "Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ That is: I am emigrating to wherever my Lord has commanded me, as he said: "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord" (Q. 29:26), and that place is al-Sham (Syria), or to wherever I may devote myself to His worship, exalted is He. ﴿He will guide me﴾ That is: to what holds the welfare of my religion, or to my destination. The firm assertion of this [guidance] is due to the prior promise, or to the intensity of his reliance upon God, and to building upon God's established practice with him. This was not the case with Musa, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way﴾ (Q. 28:22). For this reason he used the form of expectation (tawaqquʿ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 100:

﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ That is: [grant me] some of the righteous who will help me in the call (da'wah) and in obedience, and será a companion to me in estrangement; namely, a son. This is because the term "hibah" (gift), when used without qualification, is specific to a child, although it has come qualified by brotherhood in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We granted him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun as a prophet.﴾ And in His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 101:

﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy.﴾ This is explicit that the one given the good news of is the very one he (peace be upon him) had asked to be granted to him. Three glad tidings are gathered in it: the good news that he is a boy, that he will reach the age of puberty (hulm), and that he will be forbearing (halim). And what forbearance equals the forbearance of him (peace be upon him) when his father proposed to him the slaughter, and he said: ﴿O my father, do what you are commanded. You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ It has also been said: God did not describe the prophets (peace be upon them) with anything less than He described them with forbearance, because of the rarity of its existence, except Abraham and his son, for He, exalted is He, described the two of them with it, and their reported condition afterward is the clearest proof of that.

And the fa' (fa, "so") in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿فَلَمّا بَلَغَ مَعَهُ السَّعْيَ﴾ The *fa* here is *fasīḥah* (an "expressive" *fa*, which points to an omitted element). It indicates an omitted element, relying on the evidence of the situation and signalling that there is no need to state it explicitly (p-200), since failure to comply or delay after the good tidings is impossible. This is as in His saying ﴿فَلَمّا رَأيْنَهُ أكْبَرْنَهُ﴾ and His saying ﴿فَلَمّا رَآهُ مُسْتَقِرًّا عِنْدَهُ﴾. That is: so We gave him to him, and he grew up. When he reached the stage of being able to strive along with him in his affairs and needs, and "*maʿahu*" (with him) is connected to an omitted element indicated by "*al-saʿy*" (the striving), not to the verbal noun itself, because the complement of a verbal noun cannot precede it, nor to "*balagha*" (reached), because they did not reach that stage together. It is as if, when "*al-saʿy*" was mentioned, it was asked: "With whom?" and the answer was: "With him." Its specification is because the father is most complete in gentleness and in training, so he would not wish to subject him to it before its time. Or it is because he had asked for him for this purpose, and at that time he was thirteen years old.

﴿قالَ﴾ That is, Ibrahim, upon him be peace, said: ﴿يا بُنَيَّ إنِّي أرى في المَنامِ أنِّي أذْبَحُكَ﴾ "O my son, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you." That is: I see this very image, or it is his expression and its interpretation. It was said that he saw, on the night of *al-Tarwiyah*, as if someone was saying to him: "Indeed God commands you to slaughter this son of yours." When he woke in the morning, he pondered this throughout the day until evening, [wondering] whether this vision was from God or from Satan. Hence that day was named *Yawm al-Tarwiyah* (the Day of Reflection). When evening came, he saw the same thing again and knew that it was from God Most High. Hence that day was named *Yawm ʿArafah* (the Day of Recognition). Then he saw the same in the third night and resolved to sacrifice him, so that day was named *Yawm al-Nahr* (the Day of Sacrifice).

It was also said: when the angels gave him the tidings of a forbearing boy, he said: "Then he is the one to be sacrificed for God." When he was born and reached the limit of striving with him, it was said to him: "Fulfil your vow." The more evident and better known view is that the one addressed is Isma'il, upon him be peace, since he was the one granted after the migration (*al-muhajarah*). Also, the tidings of Ishaq that came after this are conjoined with the tidings of this boy. Also, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." One of them is his grandfather Isma'il, upon him be peace, and the other is his father ʿAbd Allah, because ʿAbd al-Muttalib vowed to sacrifice a son if God made it easy for him to dig the well of Zamzam, or if his sons reached ten. When that happened, and the arrow fell upon ʿAbd Allah, he ransomed him with a hundred camels, and for this reason the blood-money (*diyyah*) was prescribed as one hundred. Also, that event took place in Makkah, and the two horns of the ram were hung up in the Ka'bah until they were burned in the days of Ibn al-Zubayr, whereas Ishaq was not there. Also, the tidings of Ishaq were coupled with the birth of Ya'qub from him, so a command to slaughter him while he was a youth would not be fitting.

As for what is narrated: that he, upon him be the prayer and peace, was asked: "Which lineage is most noble?" and he said: "Yusuf, the truthful one of God, son of Ya'qub, Isra'il of God, son of Ishaq, the sacrificed one of God, son of Ibrahim, the friend of God," the sound position is that he, upon him be the prayer and peace, said: "Yusuf son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim," and the additions are from the narrator. What is narrated, that Ya'qub wrote to Yusuf something similar, is not established. It was also read: (*inniya*) with a fatha on the *ya'* in both places.

﴿فانْظُرْ ماذا تَرى﴾ "Then consider what you see," of opinion. He consulted him in this matter, though it was a decreed command, so that he might know what was in him regarding the trial of God Most High that had befallen him, so that he could firm his foot if he became distressed, and be secure regarding him if he submitted, and so that he might prepare himself for it, making it easier and earning reward for it by submitting to it before it came. It was also read: (*maza turi*) with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'* and a *kasrah* on the *rā'*, and with a *fatḥah* on both, in the passive voice. ﴿قالَ يا أبَتِ افْعَلْ ما تُؤْمَرُ﴾ "He said: O my father, do what you are commanded." That is: what you are commanded to do. The preposition was omitted first according to the regular rule, then the returning pronoun to the relative was omitted after it became accusative by its connection to the verb. Or both were omitted at once. Or [it means]: "Carry out your command," with the verbal noun construed as an annexation to its object, and the thing commanded being called a command.

It was also read: (*ma tu'maru bihi*) "what you are commanded with." The present form indicates that the command is connected to him, directed toward him, and continuing until the time of compliance with it. ﴿سَتَجِدُنِي إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ مِنَ الصّابِرِينَ﴾ "You will find me, God willing, among the patient," in the slaughter, or in submission to the decree of God Most High.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 103:

﴿When they had both submitted⁠﻿ (aslama)⁠﻿﴾: that is, they surrendered (istaslama) to the command of God, Exalted is He, and submitted, and humbled themselves before Him. It is said: sallama li-amri Allah (he submitted to the command of God), aslama (he submitted), and istaslama (he surrendered) have one meaning, and all three have been recited. Their root is from your saying: sallama hadha li-fulan (this became wholly his) when it became purely his, meaning it was kept free from dispute over it. The expressions sallama li-amri Allah and aslama lahu are derived from this, and their meaning is that he devoted his self purely to God and made it free (salimah) for Him. Likewise, the meaning of istaslama is that he devoted his self exclusively to Him, Exalted is He.

It is related from Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning (aslama): Abraham submitted his son, and Isma'il submitted himself. ﴿And he laid him down upon his forehead⁠﻿﴾: he threw him down on his side so that his forehead (jabin) fell upon the ground; the jabin is one of the two sides of the brow. It is also said: he turned him over onto his face by a gesture, so that he would not see in him anything that would produce a tenderness standing between him and the command of God, Exalted is He. This took place at the rock at Mina. It is also said: at the place overlooking the mosque of Mina. And it is said: at the place of sacrifice where sacrifice is performed today.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verses 104–105:

﴿And We called out to him, "O Abraham,"﴾ ﴿"You have fulfilled the vision,"﴾ by resolving to carry out what he had been commanded and by arranging its preliminaries. It is narrated that he pressed the knife with all his strength against his throat repeatedly, but it did not cut. Then he placed the knife on his nape, and the knife turned over. At that moment the call came, and the response to *lamma* ("when", the conditional particle) is omitted, to indicate that the expression cannot contain its details. It is as if it were said: what occurred, which the bounds of speech cannot encompass, was their joy and their thanks to God Most High for what He bestowed upon them, namely the removal of the trial after its onset, the granting of success in what no one had been granted the like of, the manifestation of their excellence over all the worlds through this, together with the attainment of a great reward, and other things besides. ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ This is a justification for relieving them of that distress because of their goodness. Those who permit *naskh* (abrogation) before the commanded act has taken place have cited this verse as evidence, since the Prophet, peace be upon him, was commanded to slaughter, according to the saying of God Most High: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾, and it did not come about.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verses 104–105:

﴿And We called out to him, "O Abraham,"﴾ ﴿"You have fulfilled the vision,"﴾ by resolving to carry out what he had been commanded and by arranging its preliminaries. It is narrated that he pressed the knife with all his strength against his throat repeatedly, but it did not cut. Then he placed the knife on his nape, and the knife turned over. At that moment the call came, and the response to *lamma* ("when", the conditional particle) is omitted, to indicate that the expression cannot contain its details.
