It is as if it were said: what occurred, which the bounds of speech cannot encompass, was their joy and their thanks to God Most High for what He bestowed upon them, namely the removal of the trial after its onset, the granting of success in what no one had been granted the like of, the manifestation of their excellence over all the worlds through this, together with the attainment of a great reward, and other things besides. ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ This is a justification for relieving them of that distress because of their goodness. Those who permit *naskh* (abrogation) before the commanded act has taken place have cited this verse as evidence, since the Prophet, peace be upon him, was commanded to slaughter, according to the saying of God Most High: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾, and it did not come about.

Indeed, this is the manifest trial (al-balaʾ al-mubin)—the clear test (al-ibtila' al-bayyin) in which the sincere one (al-mukhlis) is distinguished from others, or the evident tribulation (al-mihnah al-bayyinah), whose hardship is plain, since nothing is harder than it.

**﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾** — that is, with what would be slaughtered in his place, so that the act was completed by it. **﴿Great﴾** means either great in body and fat, or great in worth, since through it God ransomed a prophet, the son of a prophet, from whose lineage would come the master of the messengers.

It is said: that was a ram from Paradise.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that it was the ram which Abel offered, and it was accepted from him, and it kept grazing in Paradise until Isma'il, peace be upon him, was ransomed with it.

It is also said: he was ransomed with a wild goat that descended upon him from Thabir.

It is related that it fled from Abraham, peace be upon him, at the Jamra, so he threw seven pebbles at it until he caught it, and this remained a sunnah in stoning.

It is related that he threw stones at Satan when Satan came to him with whisperings at the slaughter of his son.

It is related that when he had slaughtered him, Gabriel, peace be upon him, said: "God is greatest, God is greatest." The one being sacrificed said: "There is no god but God, and God is greatest." Abraham said: "God is greatest, and to God belongs all praise." So this remained a sunnah. The actual ransomer, however, was Abraham. The phrase "And We ransomed him" was used because God, exalted is He, is the One who granted it and commanded it, by way of metaphorical usage in the ransoming or in the attribution.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 37, verses 108–109:**

﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Abraham﴾. Its explanation has already passed at the conclusion of the story of Noah, upon him be peace.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 37, verses 108–109:**

﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Abraham﴾. Its explanation has already passed at the conclusion of the story of Noah, upon him be peace.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 110:

(p-202) ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ "Dhalika" (that/thus) is a reference to the perpetuation of his good remembrance among the nations, not to what was indicated in what preceded, so there is no repetition. And the sentence is not introduced with "inna" (indeed) because of being content with what has passed just now.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 111:**

﴿Indeed, he was among Our servants, the believers﴾, those firmly established in faith, with certainty and tranquility of heart.

*Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 112:*

﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ That is: decreed for him to be a prophet, his being among the righteous having been determined. On this basis the two words (nabiyyan, "a prophet," and min al-salihin, "from among the righteous") are circumstantial clauses (hal, "circumstantial accusative"). There is no need for the one who is given the good news of to exist at the time of the good news, for the existence of the one described by the circumstantial clause is not a condition; the condition is only that the action's connection to him is contemporaneous, in view of the meaning of the circumstantial clause. Therefore there is no need to posit an omitted noun (mudaf) that would be made the governing element for both, as in "and We gave him the good news of Isaac's existence as a prophet from among the righteous." Even so, this does not become like the words of the Exalted: ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾, for those who enter were determining their abiding at the time of entering, whereas Isaac, peace be upon him, was not determining his own prophethood and righteousness at the moment he came into existence.

Whoever interprets the boy as Isaac makes the purpose of the good news his prophethood, peace be upon him. The mention of righteousness afterward is an exaltation of his station and an indication that he is the ultimate goal of it, since it includes the meaning of perfection and of perfecting others by action in an absolute sense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 113:

﴿And We blessed him﴾ — upon Ibrahim, in his offspring — ﴿and Ishaq﴾ — by bringing forth from his loins prophets of the Children of Israel and others, such as Ayyub and Shu'ayb, upon them be peace — or by pouring upon both of them the blessings of religion and the world. And it is read (wa-barraknā, "and We blessed" with intensive form). ﴿And of their offspring is one who is a doer of good﴾ — in his deeds, or for his own self, through faith and obedience — ﴿and one who wrongs himself﴾ — through disbelief and sins — ﴿clearly﴾, manifest in his wrongdoing. In this there is an admonition that lineage has no effect on guidance and misguidance, and that the wrongdoing of their descendants does not return upon them to diminish them or cause them any blemish.
ﷻ"And We certainly bestowed Our favour upon Moses and Aaron." That is: We conferred blessings upon them both, namely prophethood and other blessings, both religious and worldly.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 115:

﴿And We delivered them and their people﴾, who were the Children of Israel, ﴿from the great distress﴾. This is the dominion of the people of Pharaoh (Al Fir'awn) and their domination over them through various kinds of oppression and torment, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾. It has also been said that it is the drowning, but this is far-fetched, because it was not a distress and hardship upon them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 116:**

﴿And We helped them﴾, that is, the two of them (Musa and Harun) and their people, against their enemy, ﴿so they became the victors﴾ by virtue of that, ﴿over them﴾, with a victory beyond which there is no further end, after their people had been captives in their hands and subjugated, humbled under their oppressive dominion, who were inflicting upon them (p-203) the worst torment. This deliverance, although in terms of existence it was concurrent with the aforementioned help and victory, nevertheless, since in terms of meaning it is an expression of rescue from what is disliked, it was mentioned first; then (it was followed) by the help, whose meaning is realized by the mere deliverance of the one being helped from his enemy without subduing the enemy over him; then by the victory, so that the station of bestowing favour may be given its due by showing that each of these three levels is a magnificent blessing in its own right.
﴿And We gave them both﴾ after that, ﴿the Book that makes things clear﴾. That is, the eloquent one in clarity and detail, and it is the Tawrah (the Torah).

And We guided them both (﴿وَهَدَيْناهُما﴾) by that to the straight path (﴿الصِّراطَ المُسْتَقِيمَ﴾), the path that leads to truth and rectitude, with its details of the sacred laws (al-shara'i') and its branches of rulings (al-ahkam).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verses 119–120:

﴿And We left for them among the later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Moses and Aaron﴾. That is: We preserved among the later nations this good remembrance and this abundant praise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verses 119–120:

﴿And We left for them among the later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Moses and Aaron﴾. That is: We preserved among the later nations this good remembrance and this abundant praise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 121:

﴿Indeed, thus﴾ with complete recompense, ﴿do We reward the doers of good﴾ — those of whom they (Moses and Aaron) are part — not a recompense falling short of it.
The Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Indeed, they were among Our believing servants.﴾ Its explanation has already been given.

﴿And indeed, Ilyas was among the messengers.﴾ He is Ilyas son of Yasin, from the lineage of Harun, the brother of Musa, peace be upon them both, and he was sent after him. It is also said that he is Idris, because his name was recited in his place as (إدريس) and (إدراس). It was also recited as (إيليس), and it was recited as (الياس) with the hamza omitted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 124:

﴿When he said to his people: "Will you not fear (God)?"﴾ That is: [fear] the punishment of God, exalted is He.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 37, verse 125:

﴿Do you call upon Ba'l⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠?﴾ That is, do you worship him and seek good from him? Ba'l is the name of an idol that the people of Bakk, from al-Sham (Greater Syria), had. Bakk is the town known today as Ba'albakk (Baalbek).

It is said: it was made of gold, twenty cubits in height, and it had four faces. They were so captivated by it and held it in such great esteem that they assigned to it four hundred attendants (sadana, sing. sadin, custodians of the idol), and they made them prophets. The Devil would enter its belly and speak the law of misguidance, and the attendants would preserve it and teach it to the people. It is also said that al-Ba'l means "the Lord" in the language of Yemen, so the meaning is: do you worship some of the lords (bu'ul)? ﴿And you leave the best of creators﴾ (p-204). That is: and you abandon His worship. The factor requiring denunciation, which is signified by the interrogative hamza (alif of inquiry), has been alluded to here, and then it was stated explicitly by His words, exalted be He:

Allah is your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old. [Read in the accusative as an apposition (badal) to "the best of creators" (aḥsan al-khāliqīn).] It is also read in the nominative, as a new sentence (mubtada'). Mentioning His lordship over their forefathers serves to emphasize the denunciation of their abandoning His worship, and also to indicate the invalidity of their forefathers' opinions as well.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 127:

﴿So they denied him, and indeed they will be brought forth﴾ because of their denying that, ﴿[to punishment]﴾, that is: the punishment. The unqualified wording is used because the context suffices, given that in common usage "bringing forth" (al-ihdar al-mutlaq) is specific to evil.
Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾. It is an exception (istithna') from the pronoun in "muhdarun" (brought forward).

Translation:

﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Il Yasin.﴾ It is a dialectal variant of (Ilyas), like Sayna' for Sinin. It was also said that it is a plural of him, meant to refer to him and his followers, like al-Muhallabin and al-Khubaybin. Against this is that a proper noun, when made plural, must be made definite, as in the two examples. It was also read with the genitive construction of Al to Yasin, because in the Mushaf the two are written separately; thus Yasin would be the father of Ilyas.

﴿And indeed Lot was among the messengers.﴾ ﴿When We saved him﴾, i.e., remember the time of Our saving him ﴿and his family, all of them﴾. ﴿Except an old woman among those who remained behind.﴾ I.e., those who remained in the punishment, or those who passed on and perished. ﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ Indeed, in that are evident proofs of the clarity of his matter and of his being among the messengers.(p-205)

﴿And indeed Lot was among the messengers.﴾ ﴿When We saved him﴾, i.e., remember the time of Our saving him ﴿and his family, all of them﴾. ﴿Except an old woman among those who remained behind.﴾ I.e., those who remained in the punishment, or those who passed on and perished. ﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ Indeed, in that are evident proofs of the clarity of his matter and of his being among the messengers.(p-205)

And indeed you (O people of Makkah) ﴿pass by them﴾ at their dwellings in your trade journeys to Syria, and you witness the traces of their destruction, for Sodom lies on the road to Syria, ﴿in the morning﴾, entering upon the morning.

Qur'anic quotations are in ﴿ ﴾ markers. Translating the passage:

﴿And by night﴾ That is: and in the evening, or by day or by night. Perhaps they passed by a place near which the traveler departs in the morning and the one heading there passes by in the evening. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ Do you witness that and still not reason, so that you take heed from it and fear that there will befall you the same as what befell them.

And indeed Yunus was among the messengers. ﴿وَإنَّ يُونُسَ لَمِنَ المُرْسَلِينَ﴾ — "And indeed Yunus was among the messengers." It is also recited with a kasra on the nun (Yunusa, the genitive form).

Note on the recitation: the reading here is ﴿يُونُسَ﴾ with a fatha on the final letter (the accusative/oblique form of the name), while the variant reading has the kasra on the nun of ﴿يُونُسَ﴾ as the genitive form of the name, i.e. "Yunusi."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 140:

﴿When he fled﴾: i.e., he ran away. Its original meaning is fleeing from one's master (sayyid). However, since his fleeing from his people was without the permission of his Lord, its application to him was deemed fitting. ﴿To the laden ship﴾: i.e., the filled (al-mashhun, the full).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 141:

﴿Then he drew lots﴾ — fa-qara'a ahlahu (he cast lots with its people), ﴿and he was among those who were defeated﴾ — fa-sara min al-maghlubin (he became one of those overcome by the lot). Its root meaning is slipping away from the position of victory (al-mazlaq 'an maqam al-zafar).

It is narrated that when he (peace be upon him) threatened his people with punishment, he left among them before Allah commanded him to do so. He boarded the ship, and it stopped. They said: "There is a runaway slave on board." They cast lots, and the lot fell upon him. He said: "I am the runaway," and he threw himself into the water.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 142:**

﴿So the fish swallowed him﴾, meaning he swallowed him in one mouthful (*luqmah*, a morsel). ﴿And he was blameworthy﴾, meaning he entered into blame (*malamah*), or came with that for which he is blamed, or he was blaming himself (*mulīm nafsahu*). It was also read as *malīm* with a fatha on the first letter, formed from *layyim* in the same pattern as *mashīb* from *mashūb*.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 143:

﴿Had he not been one of those who glorify God﴾ (al-musabbihin), those who remember God much with glorification, throughout the duration of his life, or [had he not been one of them] in the belly of the fish, which is his saying: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾. And it has been said: [al-musabbihin means] those who pray (al-musallin), for indeed he, upon him be blessings and peace, was much given to prayer in times of ease.

ﷻ... Let me translate faithfully.

﴿Then he would have remained inside its belly until the day they are resurrected.﴾ [He would have remained] alive, and it was said: dead. In it is an exhortation to frequent remembrance (dhikr) of God, and a magnification of His station. Whoever turns to Him in ease, He takes him by the hand in hardship.

﴿So We cast him onto the open shore﴾, by causing the fish to spit him out, in a place bare of anything that covers it, such as trees or plants.

It is narrated (p-206) that the fish travelled alongside the ship with its head raised, and Yunus, peace be upon him, breathed through it and glorified God, and it did not leave them until they reached the shore, where it expelled him unharmed, nothing of him having changed, and so they embraced Islam.

It is also narrated that the fish cast him up on the shore of a town near Mosul. The duration of his stay (in the fish) is disputed: it was said forty days, it was said twenty, it was said seven, it was said three, and it was said that he remained only briefly, after which he was taken out of its belly shortly after the time at which he had been swallowed.

ʿAṭāʾ narrated that when it swallowed him, God Most High revealed to the fish: "I have made your belly a prison for him, and I did not make him food for you." ﴿And he was ailing﴾ from what had befallen him. It was said: his body became like the body of a child at the moment of birth.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 146:

﴿And We caused to grow over him﴾, i.e., above him, a shade over him, ﴿a tree of gourd (yaqtin)﴾. It is everything that spreads over the ground and does not stand upon a stalk, like the vines of melons, cucumbers and colocynth (al-handhal). It is on the pattern of yaf'il, from qatana bi-l-makan, "he stayed in the place" when he resided in it. Most of the scholars hold that it is the gourd (al-dubba'), whose leaves covered him against flies, for flies do not settle upon it. What indicates this is that it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you like pumpkin (al-qar')?" He said: "Indeed, it is the tree of my brother Yunus." It has also been said that it is the fig (al-tin), and it has been said that it is the banana (al-mawz); he was covered by its leaves, sheltered by its branches, and broke his fast on its fruits. It has also been said that he would take shade under the tree, and a wild mountain goat (wa'lah) would come to him and he would drink from its milk.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 147:

﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand﴾ — they were his people from whom he fled, and they are the people of Nineveh (Naynawa). What is meant is his earlier sending. He was first informed that he was among the messengers in general, and then informed that he had been sent to a great community. It seems that the mention of the time of his fleeing to the ship and what follows, placed between these two statements, is to remind of its cause, which was what took place between him — upon him be peace — and his people: his warning them of the punishment of God Most High, his specifying the time of its descent, and their excuses and their making their faith conditional on the appearance of its signs, as its details were explained earlier in Surat Yunus. This is so that it may be known that their faith, which will be related afterwards, did not come immediately after the sending, as is apparent from the ordering of faith upon it by the particle fa' (then), but rather after "the former and the latter" (al-lutayya wa'l-lati, i.e., after a long and varied course of events).

It is said: it is another sending to them. It is also said: it was to others, but this is not apparent. ﴿Or they increase﴾ — that is, in the view of the beholder: when he looks at them he would say, "They are a hundred thousand, or more." What is meant is the description of them as numerous. It is also read with the particle waw (wa, "and") instead of aw (or).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 148:**

﴿فَآمَنُوا﴾ means: after they witnessed the signs of the descent of the punishment, [they believed] with sincere faith. ﴿فَمَتَّعْناهُمْ﴾ means: We gave them enjoyment of the worldly life, ﴿إلى حِينٍ﴾ (until a time), a term which Allah, glorified is He, determined for them. It has been said: perhaps the reason this story, and the story of Lot, were not concluded with the formula with which all the other narratives were concluded, is to differentiate between them and the people of the (revealed) laws (ashab al-shara'i') and the Messengers of firm resolve (uli al-'azm min al-rusul), or it is sufficient with the comprehensive peace (al-taslim) upon all the Messengers mentioned at the end of the surah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 149:

﴿So ask them﴾ At the beginning of this noble surah, God—Mighty and Majestic is He—commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to rebuke the Quraysh and to refute their doctrine of denying the Resurrection by way of questioning (istifta'). He presented the decisive proofs that affirm its inevitable reality and explained its occurrence, and the various kinds of punishment they would face at that time. He excepted from them His sincere servants and detailed the everlasting bliss that is theirs. Then He mentioned that most of the earlier peoples had gone astray before them (p-207), and that He, exalted is He, had sent warners to them in general terms. Then He related the stories of each of them in detail, explaining in each story that they were among His servants, describing them at times with sincerity (ikhlas) and at other times with faith (iman).

Then He commanded him (ﷺ) here to rebuke them by way of questioning concerning a matter that is utterly repugnant and entirely outside the bounds of reason: the false division that follows from the crooked belief they held, for they used to say, like some of the Arab tribes—Juhayna, Banu Salima, Khuza'a and Banu Maliḥ—"The angels are the daughters of God."

The "fa" (so) indicates the ordering of the command upon what preceded: that those messengers, who are the foremost of creation—upon them be blessings and peace—are His servants, for this reinforces the rebuke and makes manifest the falsehood of their corrupt doctrine. Then (He rebukes them) by what their aforementioned disbelief entails of belittling the angels by making them females. Then He nullified the root of their disbelief, which encompasses these two disbeliefs, namely the attribution of offspring to Him—glorified and exalted is He far above that with a great exaltation. He did not include it within the rebuke because the Christians share them in this. That is: ask them, ﴿Has your Lord then daughters﴾, who are the lesser of the two kinds, ﴿and they have sons﴾, who are the superior of the two? For that is something that no one with even a little intellect would affirm.

And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 150:

﴿Or did We create the angels as females?﴾ This is an iḍrāb (a turning away from one point to another), and a transition from rebuking them by the earlier question to rebuking them with this, as has been indicated. That is: "Rather, did We create the angels, who are among the noblest of creation and the furthest of them from the attributes of bodies and the vile qualities of natures, as females? Femaleness is among the basest attributes of animals."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they were witnesses﴾ is a mockery of them and a declaration of their ignorance, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves﴾. For matters of this kind are not known through observation, since there is no way to know them through reason, and the absence of transmitted report concerning them is beyond doubt. Therefore the one who claims that they are females must have been a witness at their creation.

The clause is either a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to the subject of (We created), meaning: "Rather, did We create them as females while they were present at that time?", or it is a conjunction with (We created), meaning: "Rather, were they witnesses?"

And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verses 151–152:

﴿Surely it is from their own fabrication that they say﴾ ﴿"Allah has begotten offspring."﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) from Him, not included under the command to "ask for their opinion" (al-istifta'), and it is brought to nullify the root of their corrupt doctrine by clarifying that its foundation is nothing but plain lying (ifk) and ugly invention (iftira'), without them having any proof or even a doubt-based justification (shubhah) in the matter. ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ in their saying that, a clear lie about which there is no doubt. It is also read: (Walad Allah) ["Allah's offspring" with a short vowel on walad], as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: "The angels are His offspring," exalted is He far above that, a great exaltation. For walad is a form (fa'al) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), in which the singular, the plural, the masculine and the feminine are all alike.

Translation of Abu al-Su'ud's commentary on Surah al-Saffat, verse 153:

﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ This is a refutation of their falsehood and an affirmation of their lie in what they said, by clarifying that it entails a matter whose impossibility is evident: that He, exalted is He, chose daughters over sons. Al-istifa' (choosing) means taking the best part of a thing for oneself. It is also read with a kasra on the hamza, with the interrogative particle omitted, relying on the context as an indication of it (p-208). Making it a substitute (badal) for "and He has begotten a son (walada Allah)" is weak, and the assumption of an implied verb, i.e., "they are liars in their saying 'He has chosen...'" and so on, is a far-fetched strained interpretation.
﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ With this judgment, whose falsehood is evident to the intellect at first sight (badihat al-'aql).

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ — with one of the two tā' elided from tatadhakkarūn (تَتَذَكَّرُونَ). It is also read (tadhkurūn) (تَذْكُرُونَ), from dhakara. The fā' (الفاء) here is for conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon an implied clause, i.e., "Do you not notice this, so that you do not remember its falsehood?", for it is firmly rooted in the intellect of every intelligent and dull person alike.

Or do you have a clear authority (sultan mubin)? This is a turning away from their rebuke and reproach over what has been mentioned, to rebuking them by imposing upon them something that does not fall within existence at all. That is, rather: do you have a clear proof that has descended upon you from the heavens, stating that the angels are His daughters? For a judgment of that kind must have a sensory or rational basis, and since both are absent, there must be a transmitted basis.

"Then bring your Book, if you are truthful" (﴿فَأْتُوا بِكِتابِكُمْ﴾ — the Book that testifies to the validity of your claim, ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾ — if you are truthful in it).

In these verses there is an indication of great wrath, a terrible denunciation of their sayings, a severe dismissal of their falsehoods, a mockery of their intellects, a belittling of their understanding and minds, together with ridicule of them and wonder at their ignorance, which is not hidden from one who reflects upon them.

And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 158:

﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship.﴾ This is a shift to the third person (iltifat ila al-ghaybah) to indicate their cutting off from the answer, their falling from the rank of being addressed, the requirement of their condition that they be turned away from, and that their crimes be related to others. By "the jinn" (al-jinnah) is meant the angels. It was said: the kind is one, but whoever among the jinn is corrupt, rebellious, and entirely evil is a devil (shaytan), and whoever among them is pure, devout, and entirely good is an angel (malak).

The reason they were referred to by that name (al-jinnah), as a lowering of them and a belittling of them, despite their great standing among creation, is that they might reach the station of the kinship which they ascribed to them. Thus their making this is an expression of their saying: "The angels are the daughters of God." The mention was repeated as a preparation for what follows it, the words of His, exalted is He: ﴿And the jinn have certainly known that they will be brought forth [to punishment].﴾ That is: by God, the jinn whom they magnified by making between them and Him, exalted is He, a kinship—and they are the angels—have certainly known that the disbelievers will be brought forth to the Fire, tormented by it, because of their lying and fabrication in their saying that.

The purpose of this is to intensify the refutation by showing that those to whom these people ascribe that kinship—and who know that they are more knowledgeable than them about the reality of the matter—deny them in that, and judge with a emphatic judgment that they are tormented on account of it.

It was said: a people among the zindiqs say: God, exalted is He, and Iblis are brothers; God is the Good and the Generous, and Iblis is the Evil and the Base. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship.﴾ Imam al-Razi said: this saying, in my view, is the nearest of the sayings, and it is the doctrine of the Magians who speak of Yazdan and Ahriman, and they express them by Light and Darkness.

Mujahid said: Quraysh said: "The angels are the daughters of God." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Then who are their mothers?!"—as a rebuke to them. They said: "The chiefs of the jinn."

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ is that they made a affinity between them, in that they associated with Him, exalted is He, the jinn in deserving worship. According to these ssayings, it is permissible that the pronoun in ﴿they will be brought forth﴾ refers to the jinn, so the meaning is: the devils have known that God, exalted is He, will bring them forth to the Fire and torment them with it, and had they been akin to Him, exalted is He, or partners in deserving worship, He would not have tormented them. The first aspect is the correct one, for His saying:

﴿Glory be to God, above what they describe.﴾ This is a narration (ḥikāyah) of the angels' declaring God far exalted above what the polytheists attribute to Him, after the polytheists had denied the angels' account in that matter. It is by supposing an implied verb of saying (qawl), conjoined to the verb ﴿عَلِمَتْ﴾ ("ʿalimat," "knew") in the preceding verse.

And His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 160:

﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah.﴾ This is a testimony from them (the angels) to the innocence of the sincere ones (al-mukhlasin) from being described by Him, exalted is He, with that; it implicitly includes their disassociation from it by virtue of their inclusion in the company of the sincere ones, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. It is an exception of disconnection (istithna' munqati', an exception not belonging to the same category as what precedes it) from the waw of "yasifun" (they describe), as if it were said: "The angels certainly knew that the polytheists will indeed be punished for their saying that, and they said: 'Glory be to Allah above what they describe Him with, but the servants of Allah, of whom we are a part, are innocent of that description.'"

And His exalted saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verses 161–162:

﴿So indeed you, and what you worship﴾ ﴿you cannot lead astray [anyone] against Him﴾. This is a causal statement and a confirmation of the innocence of the sincere servants (al-mukhlisin) from what was mentioned, by explaining their inability to mislead and misguide them. The shift to direct address (al-iltifat ila al-khitab) serves to demonstrate the utmost concern with establishing the content of the speech. "Ma ta'budun" (what you worship) is an expression referring to the devils (al-shayatin) who led them astray, and in it is an indication of their disassociation from them and from their worship, like their saying: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾. "Ma" is negative (nafiyah), and "antum" is an address to them and to their objects of worship, by way of prevalence (taghlib). "'Ala" is connected to "fatinin" (tempters/seducers). It is said: "Fulan fatana 'ala fulan imra'atahu," meaning: he corrupted his wife against him (af'sadaha 'alayhi). The meaning is: indeed you, and your objects of worship, O polytheists, are not able to be tempters against Him, the Exalted, by corrupting His servants and leading them astray.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 163:

﴿Except for him who is destined to burn in Hell﴾ from among them, that is, one who will enter it, since God, exalted is He, knows that he will persist in disbelief by his own wretched choice, and will certainly become one of the people of the Fire.

As for the sincere ones (al-mukhlasun) among them, you have no power to corrupt or mislead them, so they are—without doubt—free from being tempted by you and from following your path in describing Him, exalted is He, with what you have described Him. It is also read ﴿ṣāl﴾ with a ḍammah on the lām, on the basis that it is a plural construed in accordance with the meaning of ﴿man﴾ (who), whose waw has been dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters.

And the words of God, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 164:

﴿And there is none of us but has a known station.﴾ This is a clarification of the clear state of their affair, and a specification of their place in the station of servitude, after what was mentioned of the disbelievers' lying about what they said, and the glorification of Allah Most High above that, and the absolving of the sincere servants from it, and a manifestation of the inferiority of their rank and lowliness.

That is: "And there is none of us but has a known station in worship and in submission to the command of Allah Most High, confined to him, which he does not exceed, and which he cannot leave; in submission to His greatness, humility before His awe, and modesty before His majesty, as has been related. So among them is one who bows and does not straighten his back, and one who prostrates and does not raise his head."

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "There is not a span's space in the heavens but there is an angel upon it, either praying or glorifying (Allah)."

It has been related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. By Him in whose hand my soul is, there is not a place the width of four fingers in it but there is an angel upon it, placing his forehead in prostration to Allah Most High."

And al-Suddi said: "'None of us but has a known station' in nearness (to Allah) and in witnessing (Him)."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 165:

﴿وَإنّا لَنَحْنُ الصّافُّونَ﴾ in the stations of obedience and the places of service.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 166:

﴿And indeed, we are the ones who glorify (Allah)﴾ — the ones who sanctify Allah, exalted is He, above everything that is not fitting for the majesty of His greatness. The embellishment of their speech with the various forms of emphasis (tahkid) serves to make clear that its issuing from them is with complete eagerness and vigour. This is what the sublime eloquence of the Revelation (al-tanzil) requires. Other aspects have been mentioned in the explanation (tafsir) and the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of these noble verses, so reflect on them. And Allah is the One who grants success.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 167:

﴿وَإِنْ كَانُوا لَيَقُولُونَ﴾ "In" is the lightened form of the heavy "inna" (in), the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n) is omitted, and the "lam" is the differentiating lam (al-lam al-fariqa), meaning: indeed the matter was that the Quraysh used to say:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 168:

﴿Had we had with us a reminder (dhikr) from the earlier peoples﴾ i.e., a book from the books of the earlier peoples, namely the Torah (al-Tawrat) and the Gospel (al-Injil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 169:

﴿Had we been given a reminder from the ancients, we would surely have been sincere servants of Allah.﴾ That is: we would have made worship purely for Allah the Exalted, and we would not have opposed Him as they opposed Him. This is like their saying: ﴿If a warner had come to us, we would surely have been better guided than any (other) of the nations﴾. And the "fa'" (fa, the particle of consequence) in His saying, exalted is He:

**﴿So they disbelieved in it﴾** is a *fa-fasiha* (a particle indicating an implied condition), as in His saying, ﴿Then We said: "Strike the sea with your staff," and it parted﴾ (26:63). The meaning is: then there came to them a Reminder, and what a Reminder it was, the foremost of reminders, and a Book overseeing all the other books and scriptures. **So they disbelieved in it. ﴿But they will soon know﴾**, that is, the outcome of their disbelief and its calamity.

And indeed Our word has already preceded for Our servants, the messengers.

This is a resumptive statement (istinaf) confirming the threat, and its introduction with an oath (qasam) is for the utmost care in establishing its content. That is: "By Allah, Our promise of support and victory for them has indeed preceded," and this is His, the Exalted's, statement:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verses 172–173:

﴿Indeed, they are the ones who will be given victory﴾ ﴿And indeed Our host, they are the ones who will be the victors﴾ (p-211) — namely, the followers of the messengers. ﴿They are the ones who will be the victors﴾ over their enemies in this world and the Hereafter. Their defeat in some encounters does not detract from this, for the foundation and basis of their affair is victory and triumph, even if some trial and tribulation befall them along the way, since the judgment belongs to the victor.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father): "If they are not helped in this world, they will be helped in the Hereafter."

It is also recited as ﴿ʿalā ʿabdinā﴾ ("concerning Our servant"), with the verb "sabaqat" (ﷻ-given sense: "it preceded") being construed in the sense of "ḥaqqat" (it was established). The naming of it as a "word" (kalimah), although they are "words" (kalimāt), is because they are unified in one meaning. It is also recited as ﴿kalimātunā﴾ ("Our words").

﴿Indeed, they are the ones who will be given victory﴾ ﴿And indeed Our host, they are the ones who will be the victors﴾ (p-211) — namely, the followers of the messengers. ﴿They are the ones who will be the victors﴾ over their enemies in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, disregard them and be patient, ﴿for a time﴾, until a short period, which is the period of refraining from fighting. It is said: [it refers to] the Day of Badr, and it is said: [it refers to] the Day of the Conquest.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 175:

﴿And watch them﴾ upon the worst of conditions and the most dreadful of punishments that befall them of killing and captivity. The intent of the command to watch them is to signal the utmost nearness of it, as if it were right before him.

﴿But they will see﴾ what will then befall them of matters. And "sawfa" (soon/will) here is for threat, not for distancing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 176:

﴿Will they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ It is related that when ﴿But they will see, and you will see﴾ was revealed, they said: "When will this be?" Then this was revealed.

Then when it descends upon their courtyard, that is, when the promised punishment descends upon their open space, as if it were an army that attacked them, suddenly alighting in their courtyard and launching the raid against them, cutting off their remnant completely. It was also said that the intended meaning is the descent of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the Day of Conquest. It is also read as ﴿نَزَلَ بِساحَتِهِمْ﴾ with the verb attributed to the prepositional phrase, and it is read as ﴿نُزِّلَ﴾ in the passive voice from the verb "to send down," meaning that the punishment was sent down.

﴿Evil is the morning of those who were warned﴾: then evil is the morning of those who were warned, meaning their morning. The lam here is the lam of genus (lam al-jins), and "morning" is used metaphorically, borrowed from the morning of an army that raids at dawn, for the time of the descent of the punishment. Because their raids were frequently carried out in the morning, they called them "morning," even when they happened at night.

It is narrated that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Khaybar, and they had gone out to their farms carrying their shovels, they said: "Muhammad and the army!" He drove them back to their fortress, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: ﴿God is greatest. Khaybar is ruined. Indeed, when we descend upon a people's courtyard, evil is the morning of those who were warned.﴾

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verses 178–179:**

﴿And turn away from them for a while.﴾ ﴿And watch, for they will [soon] see.﴾ This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), following upon a previous consolation, and a confirmation of the certainty of the promised appointment, coming right after another confirmation. Moreover, leaving the two verbs without an object carries the indication that what the Prophet (ﷺ) will see at that time of the various kinds of outcome, and what they will see of the different types of harm, cannot be encompassed by description or explanation. It has also been said that the first refers to the punishment of this world, and the second to the punishment of the Hereafter.

(p-212) ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe﴾. This is a declaration of the transcendence of God, exalted is He, above everything the polytheists attribute to Him that is unfitting for the majesty of His greatness and His dominion, of what is mentioned in this noble surah, and of what is not mentioned, among which is the failure to fulfil the promise made according to His preceding word, especially with regard to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This is indicated by the mention of the title "Lord" (al-Rububiyyah), which implies nurturing, perfecting, and comprehensive ownership, combined first with the pronoun referring to him (ﷺ), and second with "might" (al-'Izzah). It is as if it were said: Glory be to Him who is your Nurturer, your Perfecter, and the Owner of might and dominance absolutely, above what the polytheists attribute to Him, among which is that He abandons your victory over them, as their demand for the punishment indicates. And His, exalted is He, saying:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 37, verse 181:**

﴿And peace be upon the messengers.﴾ It is an honouring of them, peace be upon them, after His exalting Himself, the Most High, above what was mentioned (*tanzih*, declaring God free of imperfection), and an elevation of their status (*tanwih*), and a declaration that they are safe from every hardship and successful in attaining all their aims. And His saying, the Most High:

The praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds. This is an indication of His being described by His noble affirmative attributes, after the reminder that He is characterized by all His negative attributes. It also signals that His actions, which are beautiful, follow from those attributes. Among these actions is His bestowal upon them of the various sublime honours and religious and worldly perfections, and His lavishing upon them and upon those who follow them the many kinds of blessings, both apparent and hidden, which necessitate praising Him, exalted is He. It also conveys that what He promised His Messenger (ﷺ) of victory and triumph has come to pass. The purpose is to alert the believers to the manner of glorifying and praising Him, exalted is He, and to sending peace upon His messengers, who are the intermediaries between them and Him, mighty and exalted, in the outpouring of religious and worldly perfections upon them. Perhaps the placing of the greeting of peace upon the messengers between the glorification and the praise of Him is to conclude the noble surah with praise of Him, together with what this implies: that Allah's enabling of them to greet the messengers is among His blessings that necessitate praise.

From Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): Whoever wishes to be measured out with the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let his last words when he rises from his gathering be: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites As-Saffat, he will be given the reward of ten good deeds for the number of every jinn and devil, the rebellious devils will keep far from him, he will be cleared of shirk, and his two guardian angels will testify for him on the Day of Resurrection that he was a believer in the messengers."
